text: After embedding, a sentence is a stack of vectors, one per token, and the order of that stack carries meaning. The first design that read such sequences well was the recurrent neural network. It reads one token at a time and carries a memory vector called the hidden state, rather like reading a book while keeping a running summary on a single index card, which you rewrite after every word.

The rewrite rule is one line. The new hidden state mixes the old one, through a weight matrix, with the current token's vector, through a second matrix, adds a bias, and passes the result through tanh, a function that squashes any number into the range between minus one and one, so the memory can never blow up. The crucial detail is that the same weights are used at every step, which is why one small network can read a sentence of any length.

If we unroll the loop and draw every step side by side, the network becomes a long chain of identical cells, each handing its memory to the next. At every position, the hidden state can be read out to predict the following token. Training works by backpropagation through this unrolled chain, so the error signal from a late prediction has to travel backwards, cell by cell, to reach the words that caused it.

That journey backwards is where recurrent networks struggled. Each step back multiplies the gradient by the same recurrent weights and by the slope of tanh, which is never larger than one. When those factors are a little below one, the signal fades geometrically, like a photocopy of a photocopy that grows fainter with every generation; when they are a little above one, it explodes instead. Either way, the network finds it very hard to learn that a word far back in the sentence mattered.

Gated variants, the long short term memory and the gated recurrent unit, added a protected path through which information can travel with little change, much like a conveyor belt running alongside the chain, and they made recurrent networks the standard for translation for several years. Two deeper limits remained, though. Each step must wait for the previous one, so training cannot be spread across a long sequence in parallel. And everything the model knows about the past has to squeeze through one fixed size vector.

The fix began as an add on. Translation models were given a way to look back directly at every earlier position, instead of relying only on the index card. That mechanism, called attention, worked so well that a later design threw the recurrence away entirely and kept only attention, and that design is the transformer. The next lesson asks the question at its heart: which words should look at which.
